content: Benjamin Franklin often traveled with his usual companion, Sir John Pringle. His groundbreaking discoveries in electricity gained widespread recognition in France, leading to introductions to influential scientists, politicians, and even King Louis XV. While residing in London in 1768, Franklin developed a phonetic alphabet, detailed in his work A Scheme for a New Alphabet and a Reformed Mode of Spelling. This alphabet eliminated six letters he deemed redundant (c, j, q, w, x, and y) and introduced six new letters to represent sounds lacking their own symbols. However, this reformed alphabet failed to gain traction, and Franklin eventually abandoned the project. In 1771, Franklin embarked on extensive travels across the British Isles, staying with notable figures such as Joseph Priestley and David Hume. During his visit to Dublin, he was invited to sit with members of the Irish Parliament, a rare honor for an American. While touring Ireland, Franklin was deeply affected by the widespread poverty he observed, which he attributed to the same trade regulations and laws imposed by England that governed America. He feared that similar exploitation could harm America if British colonial policies persisted. In 1773, Franklin published two of his most famous pro-American satirical essays: Rules by Which a Great Empire May Be Reduced to a Small One and An Edict by the King of Prussia. He also anonymously co-published An Abridgment of the Book of Common Prayer with Francis Dashwood, which included a funeral service reduced to six minutes to preserve the health and lives of the living. Franklin obtained private letters from Massachusetts Governor Thomas Hutchinson and Lieutenant Governor Andrew Oliver, which revealed their encouragement for London to suppress the rights of Bostonians. He sent these letters to America, escalating tensions and earning a reputation among the British as a troublemaker. Hopes for a peaceful resolution diminished as Franklin was publicly ridiculed and humiliated by the Privy Council. He left London in March 1775. By the time Franklin returned to Philadelphia on May 5, 1775, the American Revolution had begun with the battles of Lexington and Concord. The New England militia had trapped the main British army in Boston. The Pennsylvania Assembly unanimously chose Franklin as their delegate to the Second Continental Congress. In June 1776, he was appointed to the Committee of Five tasked with drafting the Declaration of Independence. Despite being temporarily incapacitated by gout, Franklin made several minor edits to Thomas Jefferson's draft. At the signing, he famously remarked in response to John Hancock's comment about unity: Yes, we must, indeed, all hang together, or most assuredly we shall all hang separately. In December 1776, Franklin was sent to France as a commissioner for the United States. He resided in a home in Passy, a Parisian suburb, donated by Jacques-Donatien Le Ray de Chaumont, a supporter of the American cause. Franklin remained in France until 1785, becoming a beloved figure in French society. Wealthy French families even adorned their parlors with his portrait. Known for his flirtatious demeanor in the French style, Franklin did not engage in any actual affairs. His diplomatic efforts were highly successful, securing a critical military alliance with France in 1778 and negotiating the Treaty of Paris in 1783. During his time in France, Franklin, a Freemason, served as Grand Master of the Lodge Les Neuf Sœurs from 1779 to 1781 and was also a Past Grand Master of Pennsylvania. In 1784, Franklin participated in a commission appointed by Louis XVI to investigate Franz Mesmer's controversial theory of animal magnetism, alongside notable figures such as Antoine Lavoisier, Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, and Jean Sylvain Bailly. Upon his return to America in 1785, Franklin was second only to George Washington in his stature as a champion of American independence. He became an abolitionist, freeing his two slaves and later serving as president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. In 1787, Franklin participated as a delegate in the Philadelphia Convention, holding an honorary position and rarely engaging in debates. He is the only Founding Father to have signed all four major documents of the United States' founding: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, the Treaty of Alliance with France, and the United States Constitution. In 1787, a group of ministers in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, proposed the establishment of a new college named in Franklin's honor. He donated £200 to support the development of what is now Franklin & Marshall College. Between 1771 and 1788, Franklin completed his autobiography, initially addressed to his son but later expanded for the benefit of humanity at a friend's request. In his later years, as Congress grappled with the issue of slavery, Franklin wrote several essays advocating for its abolition and the integration of African Americans into American society. These writings included An Address to the Public (1789), A Plan for Improving the Condition of the Free Blacks (1789), and Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim on the Slave Trade (1790). In 1790, Quakers from New York and Pennsylvania presented a petition for abolition, supported by the Pennsylvania Abolitionist Society and its president, Franklin. On November 18, 1785, Franklin was unanimously elected the sixth President of the Supreme Executive Council of Pennsylvania, a position analogous to the modern role of governor. He served for over three years, the constitutional limit of three full terms, and was re-elected twice. His term officially ended on November 5, 1788, though there is some uncertainty about his active involvement toward the end due to his advanced age. Franklin believed that the survival of the new republic depended on the virtue of its citizens, emphasizing civic duty and the rejection of corruption. Throughout his life, he explored the role of civic and personal virtue, as reflected in the aphorisms of Poor Richard's Almanack.
